name: Kolmogorov ($T_0$)
definition: For any two distinct points $x \neq y \in X$, there exists an open set containing one but not the other.
equivalentForms: The topological indistinguishability equivalence relation is the equality relation.
The closure of distinct singletons are distinct: $\overline{\{x\}} \neq \overline{\{y\}}$ for $x \neq y$.
nonExamples: An indiscrete space with more than one point
notes: Introduced by Kolmogorov in 1931. The weakest standard separation axiom.

name: Fréchet ($T_1$)
definition: For any two distinct points $x \neq y \in X$, there exists an open set containing $x$ but not $y$, and an open set containing $y$ but not $x$.
equivalentForms: Every singleton subset $\{x\}$ is closed in $X$.
The intersection of all open neighborhoods of $x$ is $\{x\}$.
examples: Cofinite topology on an infinite set

name: Hausdorff ($T_2$)
definition: For any two distinct points $x \neq y \in X$, there exist disjoint open sets $U$ and $V$ with $x \in U$ and $y \in V$.
equivalentForms: The diagonal $\Delta = \{(x, x) : x \in X\}$ is closed in $X \times X$.
Every convergent net or filter in $X$ has a unique limit.
nonExamples: Cofinite topology on an infinite set
Zariski topology on an algebraic variety of dimension $\ge 1$
notes: Introduced by Felix Hausdorff in 1914. Fundamental for analysis.

name: Regular
definition: For every closed set $C \subseteq X$ and point $x \notin C$, there exist disjoint open sets $U, V$ such that $x \in U$ and $C \subseteq V$.
equivalentForms: For every point $x$ and open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there exists an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ such that $\overline{V} \subseteq U$.
notes: Note: regularity does not require points to be closed. When combined with $T_1$, it yields $T_3$.

name: Vietoris ($T_3$)
definition: A topological space that is both Regular and $T_1$.
equivalentForms: Regular and Hausdorff ($T_2$).
Singletons are closed and every closed set and disjoint point are separated by neighborhoods.
nonExamples: Cofinite topology on an infinite set

name: Tychonoff ($T_{3\frac{1}{2}}$)
definition: A $T_1$ space where every closed set $C$ and point $x \notin C$ can be separated by a continuous function $f: X \to [0, 1]$ with $f(x) = 0$ and $f(C) = \{1\}$.
equivalentForms: Completely regular and $T_1$.
Homeomorphic to a subspace of a compact Hausdorff space (cube $[0, 1]^I$).
nonExamples: Thomas's plank (a $T_3$ space that is not completely regular)
notes: Named after Andrey Tychonoff. Essential for the theory of compactification.

name: Normal
definition: For any two disjoint closed sets $A, B \subseteq X$, there exist disjoint open sets $U, V$ with $A \subseteq U$ and $B \subseteq V$.
equivalentForms: For every closed set $A$ and open set $W \supseteq A$, there exists open $U$ with $A \subseteq U \subseteq \overline{U} \subseteq W$.
notes: Does not require points to be closed. When paired with $T_1$, gives $T_4$.

name: Tietze ($T_4$)
definition: A topological space that is both Normal and $T_1$.
equivalentForms: Normal and Hausdorff ($T_2$).
Satisfies Urysohn's Lemma and Tietze Extension Theorem for closed subsets.
notes: Normal Hausdorff space. Guarantees existence of rich families of real-valued continuous functions.

name: Compact
definition: Every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.
equivalentForms: Every family of closed sets with finite intersection property has non-empty intersection.
Every ultrafilter on $X$ converges to at least one point.
notes: One of the most important concepts in modern mathematics. Discovered through generalizations of Heine-Borel.

name: Countably Compact
definition: Every countable open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.
equivalentForms: Every sequence in $X$ has an accumulation point (cluster point).
Every infinite subset has an $\omega$-accumulation point.
notes: Weaker than compact; equivalent to compactness in Lindelöf spaces.

name: Sequentially Compact
definition: Every sequence in $X$ contains a convergent subsequence.
equivalentForms: Every countably infinite set contains a sequence with a convergent subsequence.
notes: Historically the earliest form of compactness (Fréchet). Differs from compactness in non-first-countable spaces.

name: Limit Point Compact
definition: Every infinite subset of $X$ has a limit point in $X$ (Bolzano-Weierstrass property).
equivalentForms: Weakly countably compact.
Every countably infinite subset has an accumulation point.
notes: In $T_1$ spaces, this is equivalent to countable compactness (Munkres Theorem 28.1).

name: Lindelöf
definition: Every open cover of $X$ has a countable subcover.
equivalentForms: Every family of closed sets with countable intersection property has non-empty intersection.

name: First Countable
definition: Every point $x \in X$ has a countable local base of neighborhoods.
equivalentForms: For each $x$, there exist open sets $U_1, U_2, \dots$ such that any neighborhood of $x$ contains some $U_n$.
notes: Allows sequences to fully characterize closure, continuity, and limit points.

name: Second Countable
definition: The topology of $X$ has a countable base of open sets.
equivalentForms: There exists a countable collection $\mathcal{B}$ of open sets such that every open set is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Euclidean topology (open balls with rational centers and radii)
notes: Implies both first countability and the Lindelöf property.

name: Metrizable
definition: There exists a metric $d$ on $X$ that induces the given topology.
equivalentForms: Regular Hausdorff space with a $\sigma$-locally finite base (Nagata-Smirnov Metrization Theorem).
$T_3$ and second countable (Urysohn Metrization Theorem).
nonExamples: Cofinite topology on an infinite set
notes: Metrizability theorems (Urysohn, Nagata-Smirnov, Bing) are central achievements of point-set topology.
